specPoints.text: understand how random fertilisation produces genetic variation of offspring

primer.text: Variation has a second engine beyond meiosis. This note adds the lottery of fertilisation: any sperm can meet any egg, so every zygote assembles a fresh allele combination, and the resulting differences — blood group, eye colour, tongue rolling, earlobes — show up across whole families.

lessons.title: The Fertilisation Lottery
lessons.opening: Meiosis already shuffles the gametes an individual makes, and fertilisation shuffles again: any sperm can meet any egg, so each zygote assembles a unique allele combination, which is why siblings differ in blood group, eye colour and the rest.
keyPoints: Meiosis creates genetic variation among the gametes one individual produces.
Each gamete carries a substantially different set of alleles.
Any sperm can meet any egg when fertilisation happens.
Random fusion gives each zygote a unique allele combination.
Blood group, eye colour, tongue rolling and earlobes illustrate the variation.

low.restatement: Random pairs of unlike gametes make zygotes that are all genetically different.
low.analogy: Two shuffled decks cut at random: every hand differs.
low.examPointer: Credit meiosis for gamete variety and fertilisation for the pairing.

medium.restatement: The uniqueness of each zygote follows from two independent random draws, gamete by gamete.
medium.analogy: A two-drum lottery: one number from each drum, drawn fresh each time.
medium.examPointer: Quote the human examples to finish a full-mark answer.

options.text: Any sperm cell can meet any egg cell
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.
No selection among gametes is implied.
Parents control nothing at this stage.

check.stem: Why do gametes differ from one another before fertilisation?

options.text: Meiosis has already produced genetic variation between them
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.
Mitosis is not the gamete-maker.
Mutation is random, never purposeful.
Fertilisation happens after the variety exists.

options.text: A unique combination of alleles from two gametes
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
Each pairing is fresh.
Paternal alleles arrive with the sperm.
Fusion restores the full diploid set.

check.stem: Which example set illustrates human genetic variation here?

options.text: Blood group, eye colour, tongue rolling and earlobes
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.
Height is taught as polygenic, not in this list.
Fingerprints are not in the taught list.
Those are environmental examples.

check.stem: Two siblings of the same parents differ in eye colour. Which process explains this best?

options.text: Random fertilisation assembling different allele combinations in each zygote
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.
Parental genotypes are fixed.
Eye colour here is genetic.
Mutation is random, never deliberate.

check.stem: State how random fertilisation produces genetic variation.
check.modelAnswer: Gametes already differ because of meiosis, and their random fusion gives every zygote a unique allele combination.

check.stem: Name two human characteristics listed as examples of genetic variation.
check.modelAnswer: Blood group and eye colour, with tongue rolling and earlobe form also given.

check.stem: Explain why siblings from the same parents are not genetically identical.
check.modelAnswer: Each conception fuses a different pair of gametes, so each child assembles a different allele combination despite sharing the same parents.

check.stem: A family has five children with three different blood groups among them. Explain how one couple can produce that variety.
check.modelAnswer: Each conception paired different gametes drawn from the parents' allele pools, so random fertilisation assembled a different allele combination, and hence a different blood group, in each child.

glossary.definition: The fusion of male and female gametes to form a zygote.
A sex cell whose alleles differ from its siblings' thanks to meiosis.
The cell formed at fertilisation, carrying a unique allele combination.
Differences in inherited alleles between individuals.
